Zerodha Broking Ltd is an Indian brokerage and financial services company, based in Bengaluru. It offers an online trading platform that facilitates institutional and retail trading of stocks, derivatives "Derivative (finance)"), currencies, commodities, mutual funds, and bonds "Bond (finance)"). It is a member of the National Stock Exchange of India (NSE), Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE), and the Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX).
Zerodha was founded and bootstrapped "Bootstrapping (business)") by brothers Nithin and Nikhil Kamath. As of May 2024, it has 7.5 million active customers registered with the NSE, making it the second-largest stockbroker in India.
History
[edit]
Zerodha was founded in August 2010 by brothers Nithin Kamath and Nikhil Kamath as a discount brokerage firm. The name Zerodha was a combination of words for the company's ideals: zero and rodha, the Sanskrit word for 'barrier'. The company started with six employees and ₹2 crore in seed money drawn from Nithin Kamath's personal savings and contributions from a Singapore-based friend.
Kailash Nadh joined Zerodha in 2013 to start its technology team and has served as the company's chief technology officer since then, building its trading platforms in-house. In 2019, Zerodha became the largest retail stockbroker in India by active client base, overtaking ICICI Securities. It contributed up to 2% of daily retail volumes on Indian stock exchanges at the time.
In June 2020, it became a "unicorn "Unicorn (finance)")" with a self-assigned valuation of around $1 billion based on an ESOP buyback. Zerodha had about 1.3 million customers in early 2020, which rose to nearly 10 million by the end of 2022. In 2020, Zerodha applied for a licence to set up an asset management company (AMC) in India and launched its fund house in 2023.
In November 2025, Zerodha invested in Tijori Finance, a Bengaluru-based market data and research platform. In 2026, Zerodha obtained merchant banking licence through its subsidiary Zerodha Corporate Advisors, enabling it to offer investment banking services such as managing public offerings.
Products and subsidiaries
[edit]
A fixed commission of up to ₹20 is applied to all equity trading and derivative transactions, regardless of its size. Equity delivery is commission-free. The company also offers commodity trading through its wholly owned subsidiary, Zerodha Commodities Pvt. Ltd.
Rainmatter
[edit]
In 2014, Rainmatter was founded as an early-stage fund focused on financing start-ups in new technology and new product development. Some notable investments by Rainmatter are in startups such as Cred "Cred (company)"), Finception, Smallcase, and Sensibull. The company has also backed GoldenPi and WintWealth, which are bond "Bond (finance)") purchasing platforms.
True Beacon
[edit]
In 2019, Zerodha started True Beacon, an alternative investment fund (AIF) with a defensive investment strategy.
Zerodha Fund House
[edit]
In October 2023, Zerodha launched Zerodha Fund House, an AMC, in partnership with Smallcase. It focused on index funds and had only direct plans which paid no commissions to distributors. In March 2024, the fund house had an AUM of ₹10 billion (US$100 million).
FLOSS Fund
[edit]
On 15 October 2024, Zerodha announced the launch of FLOSS Fund dedicated to Free/Libre and Open Source projects globally. Zerodha committed to giving up to $1 million per year to support developers and communities that create and maintain such projects.
Technical problems and interruptions
[edit]
There have been multiple reports of technical issues, including glitches, system outages, and connectivity issues on Zerodha's Kite platform, especially on days with high market volatility and F&O expiry days.
In November 2020, Livemint reported that some Zerodha traders complained of being unable to access its Kite platform due to a technical issue. Several users took to Twitter to report a login issue. Zerodha, in an official statement, acknowledged the problem.
Awards
[edit]
 They were recognised with the award 'Retail Brokerage of the year 2018', by National Stock Exchange.
 Outlook Money recognised Zerodha with 'Retail Broker of the year' award in 2017.
 In 2017, they were also awarded the 'Young Entrepreneur of the Year (Startup) Award' by Ernst and Young.

Trading Q&A
We pioneered the discount broking model in India. Now, we are breaking ground with our technology.
We kick-started operations on the 15th of August, 2010 with the goal of breaking all barriers that traders and investors face in India in terms of cost, support, and technology. We named the company Zerodha, a combination of Zero and "Rodha", the Sanskrit word for barrier.
Today, our disruptive pricing models and in-house technology have made us the biggest stock broker in India.
Over 1.8+ crore clients place billions of orders every year through our powerful ecosystem of investment platforms, contributing over 15% of all Indian retail trading volumes.
In addition, we run a number of popular open online educational and community initiatives to empower retail traders and investors.
Rainmatter, our fintech fund and incubator, has invested in several fintech startups with the goal of growing the Indian capital markets.
And yet, we are always up to something new every day. Catch up on the latest updates on our blog or see what the media is saying about us or learn more about our business and product philosophies.

Profile · Nithin Kamath
Nithin Kamath: Zerodha Founder's Biography
Nithin Kamath, born 1979 in Shivamogga: how a call-centre worker and trader bootstrapped Zerodha, brother Nikhil, wife Seema Patil, and his net worth.
CapitalVia Research Desk · · 45 min read
Nithin Kamath, founder and CEO of Zerodha, 2020
Nithin Kamath, founder and CEO of Zerodha, 2020. Photo: Karthik Rangappa, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.jpg)
| Key facts |

| Born | 1979, Shivamogga (Shimoga), Karnataka (published profiles give 5 October 1979) |
| Family roots | Konkani family; father U. R. Kamath spent his career at Canara Bank; mother Revathi taught the veena (#source-44 "Zerodha's Nithin Kamath acknowledges father's role in the Kamath brothers' success - Storyboard18, Dec 2023") (#source-2 "I am Nithin, and I founded Zerodha - nithinkamath.me, Jan 2021") |
| Education | Engineering studies at Bangalore Institute of Technology; by his own account he never cleared the backlog of papers needed for the degree (#source-30 "The Back Office conversation with Karthik - nithinkamath.me, Sep 2026") |
| Family | Married to Seema Patil, a whole-time director of Zerodha; younger brother Nikhil Kamath is Zerodha’s co-founder (#source-1 "About Zerodha - Zerodha, Oct 2026") (#source-72 "Exclusive: Kamath brothers and Seema Patil to get up to Rs 100 Cr as salary - Entrackr, May 2021") |
| Company/Group | Zerodha Broking Ltd (founder and CEO); Zerodha Fund House; Rainmatter (startup investments and climate foundation) |
| Wealth | About US$4.7 billion (Forbes real-time, 13 Oct 2026) (#source-37 "Nithin Kamath (real-time net worth profile) - Forbes, Oct 2026"); “Nithin Kamath & family” Rs 40,020 crore, rank 64 (Hurun India Rich List 2025) (#source-98 "Ambani tops Hurun India Rich List 2025: top 100 richest Indians - Trak.in, Oct 2025") (#source-99 "Bengaluru's billionaire list: Azim Premji, Nithin Kamath and others - StartupTalky, Oct 2025") |
| Known for | Building India’s first big discount broker without outside funding, advertising or a sales team; zero brokerage on stock investing; Varsity; Rainmatter |
Where it began
In September 2011, a journalist from The Economic Times called a small Bengaluru brokerage that was promising to charge traders a flat Rs 20 an order. The person who picked up the phone was the founder himself, Nithin Kamath. But in those days he did not make sales calls as Nithin. He called himself “Sachin” and, as he later admitted, “faked a weird accent”. “You didn’t want the CEO making sales calls,” he wrote fifteen years later. “I’ve even met customers pretending to be Sachin.” (#source-29 "The first time we appeared in the press - nithinkamath.me, Sep 2026")
The one-line mention that followed was a turning point for a firm that had spent its first year chasing clients one cold call at a time. Account openings went from a few hundred a month to almost 500 (#source-29 "The first time we appeared in the press - nithinkamath.me, Sep 2026"). Fifteen years on, that firm, Zerodha, has more than 1.8 crore clients (#source-1 "About Zerodha - Zerodha, Oct 2026"), earned a profit of about Rs 4,283 crore in 2025-26 (#source-62 "Zerodha's bland FY26: net profit up a mere 1% - Inc42, Aug 2026") (#source-63 "Zerodha marks 16 years with steady profits - YourStory, Aug 2026"), and has never taken a rupee of venture capital (#source-33 "Inside the making of Zerodha - Nithin Kamath (Substack), Jul 2026").
The man behind it is not an IIT or IIM graduate. He did not finish his engineering degree. He spent four years making unsolicited calls to Americans from a call centre at night while trading stocks by day, after blowing up his own trading account. This is that story.
A banker’s son in Shivamogga
Nithin Kamath was [personal detail removed]ily (#source-47 "No IIM or Harvard: how Nithin Kamath built Zerodha without a management degree - Business Today, Nov 2022") (#source-35 "Nithin is a bull tamer in his own right (The New Indian Express, reposted) - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Jan 2013"). His father, U. R. Kamath, “worked his entire life” at Canara Bank (#source-44 "Zerodha's Nithin Kamath acknowledges father's role in the Kamath brothers' success - Storyboard18, Dec 2023"), which meant regular transfers; the family eventually settled in Bangalore when his father was posted there (#source-46 "New Money Multipliers - Entrepreneur India, Apr 2022"). His mother, Revathi, taught the veena (#source-2 "I am Nithin, and I founded Zerodha - nithinkamath.me, Jan 2021"). Nikhil, his younger brother, would later become his partner.
“Being the son of a bank manager, I learnt about the importance of money at an early age,” Kamath wrote in 2012. “In fact, I had to earn my pocket money right through college.” (#source-34 "The Economic Times, 29 Oct 2012 (first-person piece, reposted) - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Oct 2012")
He is frank about school. “In school, I was a below average student academically,” he says on his personal website (#source-2 "I am Nithin, and I founded Zerodha - nithinkamath.me, Jan 2021"). What caught him instead was the stock market. Some friends in his Bangalore neighbourhood came from Marwari trading families, and through them he discovered shares (#source-35 "Nithin is a bull tamer in his own right (The New Indian Express, reposted) - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Jan 2013"). “I discovered trading and the markets by accident at the age of 17,” he writes (#source-2 "I am Nithin, and I founded Zerodha - nithinkamath.me, Jan 2021"). Most accounts put this at about 1996-97 (#source-41 "Meet the Mavericks: Nithin Kamath - YourStory, Jul 2019") (#source-40 "From trading alone at the age of 17 to starting up Zerodha - YourStory, Nov 2012"); an early newspaper profile says 16 (#source-35 "Nithin is a bull tamer in his own right (The New Indian Express, reposted) - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Jan 2013").
His father gave him his first trading capital (#source-44 "Zerodha's Nithin Kamath acknowledges father's role in the Kamath brothers' success - Storyboard18, Dec 2023"). In those pre-internet days newspapers were his only research tool, and he traded mostly small, cheap stocks (#source-34 "The Economic Times, 29 Oct 2012 (first-person piece, reposted) - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Oct 2012") (#source-41 "Meet the Mavericks: Nithin Kamath - YourStory, Jul 2019").
Engineering, on paper
He enrolled for engineering at Bangalore Institute of Technology, under Bangalore University (#source-34 "The Economic Times, 29 Oct 2012 (first-person piece, reposted) - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Oct 2012"). Many profiles say he graduated in 2001. His own account, written in September 2026, is different. He and his friend Karthik Rangappa, he says, were in “the last batch at Bangalore University with the ‘all-carry’ system”, where students could move up years with papers still pending. “I basically had 45-odd subjects to write by the 8th semester, and I never wrote them.” (#source-30 "The Back Office conversation with Karthik - nithinkamath.me, Sep 2026")
So the founder of one of India’s most profitable financial firms has, by his own telling, no degree. “No IIM or Harvard,” as one business magazine put it (#source-47 "No IIM or Harvard: how Nithin Kamath built Zerodha without a management degree - Business Today, Nov 2022").
The first break
Blowing up the account
The early profits did not last. The dotcom bust of 2000-01 “nearly wiped off all that I had earned over the past four-five years”, he wrote in 2012 (#source-34 "The Economic Times, 29 Oct 2012 (first-person piece, reposted) - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Oct 2012"). YourStory, retelling his story, put the loss at about Rs 5 lakh (#source-43 "The Turning Point: what led Nithin Kamath to launch Zerodha - YourStory, Apr 2020"). His own summary is blunter: “In the early 2000s, I borrowed money and blew up my trading account.” (#source-2 "I am Nithin, and I founded Zerodha - nithinkamath.me, Jan 2021")
He also tried, and failed at, a multi-level marketing venture. His father was his first customer for that too (#source-44 "Zerodha's Nithin Kamath acknowledges father's role in the Kamath brothers' success - Storyboard18, Dec 2023"). YourStory counts two failed businesses before Zerodha (#source-42 "Matrix Moments: from trading at 17 to working at a call centre - YourStory, Mar 2020").
Night shifts at a call centre
To pay off the debt he took a night job at a call centre serving the US market, selling everything from phones to DVDs by phone (#source-42 "Matrix Moments: from trading at 17 to working at a call centre - YourStory, Mar 2020"). During the day, he kept trading.
“I spent four years at a call centre, making unsolicited calls to people in the US,” he wrote on X in May 2024, after getting a spam call himself. “I guess Karma has a way of biting back.” (#source-45 "'Karma has a way of biting back': spam calls remind Nithin Kamath of call centre days - Business Today, May 2024") Most sources date the job to roughly 2001-2005 (#source-42 "Matrix Moments: from trading at 17 to working at a call centre - YourStory, Mar 2020") (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014"). He later told The Economic Times: “I was not from a very privileged background… I used to trade in the day and work with the call centre at night.” (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014") It was also where he met Seema Patil, who later became his wife (#source-2 "I am Nithin, and I founded Zerodha - nithinkamath.me, Jan 2021").
The first client
The break came from a client, not a job. A man who had seen his trading record asked Kamath to manage his money. Accounts differ on who this was: a retired man in one interview (#source-35 "Nithin is a bull tamer in his own right (The New Indian Express, reposted) - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Jan 2013"), a person “who had come back from the US” in another (#source-46 "New Money Multipliers - Entrepreneur India, Apr 2022"). His website thanks “Prakash my first customer” (#source-2 "I am Nithin, and I founded Zerodha - nithinkamath.me, Jan 2021"). What is consistent is what happened next: “I quit my job when I met the first person who asked me to manage their portfolio.” (#source-2 "I am Nithin, and I founded Zerodha - nithinkamath.me, Jan 2021")
He set up Kamath Associates, a small advisory and portfolio business. By about 2005 he was knocking on doors trying to sell investment accounts. One of those doors belonged to Karthik Rangappa, who later “helped us build our first website… back when we were called Kamath Associates” and today runs Zerodha’s education arm (#source-30 "The Back Office conversation with Karthik - nithinkamath.me, Sep 2026").
A sub-broker at Reliance Money
In 2006 he became a franchisee, or sub-broker, of Reliance Money to formalise the business (#source-2 "I am Nithin, and I founded Zerodha - nithinkamath.me, Jan 2021") (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014"). That year Venu Madhav, now Zerodha’s chief operating officer, left “a stable, well-paying job at HP to join me back when I was just a sub-broker at Reliance Money”, Kamath wrote in 2026. “I couldn’t even guarantee him a monthly salary.” (#source-31 "The Back Office with Venu Madhav - nithinkamath.me, Aug 2026") Nikhil joined around 2007 (#source-46 "New Money Multipliers - Entrepreneur India, Apr 2022") after quitting his own call-centre job at about 20 (#source-48 "From dropout to fintech disruptor: Zerodha's Nikhil Kamath - Al Jazeera, Sep 2021"). Hanan, a trader friend who would run client support, came in 2008 (#source-13 "Our 10th anniversary and the future - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Aug 2020") (#source-2 "I am Nithin, and I founded Zerodha - nithinkamath.me, Jan 2021").
Kamath became one of Reliance Money’s largest sub-brokers; at times, YourStory reported, his volumes beat those of the other thousand-odd sub-brokers combined (#source-40 "From trading alone at the age of 17 to starting up Zerodha - YourStory, Nov 2012"). He also watched something closely. Reliance Money had launched a flat-fee plan in 2007 and then scrapped it (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014"). The idea stayed with him: “The effort needed of a broker to put in an order worth Rs 1 lakh or Rs 10 lakh is the same. Then, why should brokers charge more for bigger orders?” (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014")
In 2008, as markets crashed, he returned the deposits of his 40-odd advisory clients and decided to become a broker himself (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014").
Zero barriers
In 2009, venture capitalists he met were “dismissive” of a cheap broker run from Bengaluru (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014"). Many people asked, he later recalled, “who starts a brokerage firm in Bengaluru?” (#source-28 "The role NSE played in Zerodha's early days - nithinkamath.me, Sep 2026")
The brothers paid for it themselves, with personal savings and help from a friend in Singapore (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014"); Nikhil traded the remaining funds to extend the runway (#source-13 "Our 10th anniversary and the future - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Aug 2020"). The National Stock Exchange helped in a way Kamath still talks about. The exchange gave small brokers a free trading platform, NSE NOW, and “when they realised we didn’t have a lot of money, they even waived our membership fee of ~₹5 lakh,” he wrote. “In many ways, we are around only because of the NSE.” (#source-28 "The role NSE played in Zerodha's early days - nithinkamath.me, Sep 2026") (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014")
Zerodha began operations on 15 August 2010, India’s Independence Day (#source-1 "About Zerodha - Zerodha, Oct 2026") (#source-13 "Our 10th anniversary and the future - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Aug 2020"). The name joins “zero” and “rodha”, the Sanskrit word for barrier. “Removing all barriers for traders is what we were trying to attempt,” he explained (#source-32 "The story behind how the name Zerodha came to be - nithinkamath.me, Dec 2021"). The pitch: a flat Rs 20 per executed order, however big (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014").
It was a hard sell. “Nobody wanted to trade with an unknown entity despite cheaper brokerage,” he said (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014"). Six months and about 15,000 cold calls later, Zerodha had only about 1,000 clients (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014"). “The biggest challenge for us is credibility, because we charge so less,” he told YourStory in 2012 (#source-40 "From trading alone at the age of 17 to starting up Zerodha - YourStory, Nov 2012").
Building the empire
Slow years, 2010-2015
The first years were a grind of word of mouth. Zerodha did not advertise; from 2010 it ran a referral programme instead (#source-14 "12 years of Zerodha - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Aug 2022"). By September 2014 it had about 42,000 clients and had earned revenue of Rs 37 crore in 2013-14, with about 120 employees, many of them friends from the call-centre days (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014").
Three hires from this period shaped what came next. Kailash Nadh, a computer scientist, joined in 2013 and built Zerodha’s in-house technology team; he is now chief technology officer (#source-13 "Our 10th anniversary and the future - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Aug 2020") (#source-1 "About Zerodha - Zerodha, Oct 2026"). Karthik Rangappa came in around 2013-14 to write about markets (#source-30 "The Back Office conversation with Karthik - nithinkamath.me, Sep 2026") (#source-13 "Our 10th anniversary and the future - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Aug 2020"). And on 5 November 2014, Kamath launched Varsity, a free, plain-language online course on stock markets written by Rangappa, open to anyone, client or not (#source-11 "Introducing Varsity - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Nov 2014").
The zero-brokerage bet, 2015
The real turn came at the end of 2015. On 30 November Kamath announced that from 1 December 2015, buying shares for delivery (investing, not trading) would carry zero brokerage. Intraday and futures-and-options (F&O) trades would stay at Rs 20 or 0.01%, whichever was lower (#source-10 "Zerodha going zero brokerage - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Nov 2015"). Around the same time Zerodha launched Kite, its own fast trading platform, first released in beta in September 2015 (#source-12 "Kite - Introduction - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Sep 2015"), along with Kite Connect, a set of APIs for programmers (#source-10 "Zerodha going zero brokerage - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Nov 2015").
Free investing was a deliberate trade-off: Zerodha would earn from active traders and use free delivery to bring in long-term investors. It took about five years to win the first 60,000-odd accounts; after the zero-brokerage move growth sped up sharply (#source-46 "New Money Multipliers - Entrepreneur India, Apr 2022"). In April 2026 Kamath estimated that clients had saved about Rs 25,620 crore between 2016 and 2025 by not paying brokerage on delivery trades (#source-71 "Rs 25,620 crore saved on brokerage: what Nithin Kamath wants you to know - Business Today, Apr 2026").
Around 2015-16 Zerodha also started Rainmatter, a fund and incubator for fintech startups. The early bets included smallcase (portfolios of stocks), Sensibull (an options platform) and Streak (an algo-trading tool) (#source-24 "Approaching a decade - Z-Connect (Rainmatter), Jan 2025"). Coin, a platform for buying direct mutual funds commission-free, followed (#source-1 "About Zerodha - Zerodha, Oct 2026").
India’s No. 1 broker, 2019
By December 2018 Zerodha had 8.47 lakh active clients on the NSE, just ahead of ICICI Securities’ 8.44 lakh. A bootstrapped Bengaluru startup had become India’s largest broker by active clients (#source-49 "With 8.47 lakh clients, Zerodha takes lead as largest broker in India - YourStory, Jan 2019"). “To start a broking firm was probably a little stupid,” Kamath said the following year (#source-41 "Meet the Mavericks: Nithin Kamath - YourStory, Jul 2019").
In the 2019 annual return of Zerodha Broking Ltd, the promoters held all 10 crore shares: Nithin Kamath 30.91%, Austin Global Ventures 29.91%, Nikhil Kamath 28.91% and Seema Patil 9.97%, with token holdings for their parents (#source-3 "Zerodha Broking Ltd annual return (Form MGT-9 extract), FY2018-19 - Zerodha, 2019"). More recent shareholding details have not been widely reported; Zerodha has never raised external capital (#source-33 "Inside the making of Zerodha - Nithin Kamath (Substack), Jul 2026").
The pandemic boom, 2020-2022
When Covid-19 shut India down in 2020, millions of young people opened their first trading accounts. Zerodha was best placed to catch them.
In June 2020 it bought back employee stock options at Rs 700 a share, more than four times book value. That implied a valuation of about Rs 7,000 crore, or roughly US$1 billion: a self-declared unicorn with no investors (#source-52 "Zerodha claims unicorn valuation in ESOPs buyback plan - Inc42, Jun 2020"). “Everyone working in the company thought $1 billion was a cool number to be at,” Kamath said. Zerodha then had about 28 lakh clients and about 1,100 employees (#source-53 "Bootstrapped to billions: Zerodha, a rare profitable fintech, turns unicorn - YourStory, Jun 2020").
Profits grew fast. Kamath said profit after tax for 2020-21 was “about Rs 1,000 crore” (#source-56 "Stock broking giant Zerodha's FY21 profit more than doubles to Rs 1,000 cr - Business Standard, May 2021"). In 2021-22 revenue reached about Rs 4,964 crore and profit about Rs 2,094 crore; in 2022-23, Rs 6,875 crore and Rs 2,907 crore (#source-55 "Zerodha annual results: Nithin Kamath says 40% yearly jump in revenues in FY23 - Business Today, Sep 2023"). In September 2023 he said recent share buybacks valued Zerodha at about Rs 30,000 crore (US$3.6 billion), using 10-15 times profit, and “not the Rs 1 lakh to Rs 2 lakh crores” some people imagined (#source-54 "Zerodha valued at $3.6 Bn, says CEO Nithin Kamath - Inc42, Sep 2023").
Throughout, he refused to list the company. “As soon as you have lakhs of conservative retail investors on your cap table, the obligations go up exponentially,” he wrote in 2021, adding that an IPO “is the beginning & not the end” (#source-87 "Amidst IPO frenzy, Nithin Kamath explains why Zerodha isn't going public - OfficeChai, Nov 2021").
A different kind of broker
What made Zerodha unusual was less its prices than its restraint.
It does not advertise, does not run a sales team with targets and does not “push people to trade or invest”, Kamath wrote in 2026 (#source-33 "Inside the making of Zerodha - Nithin Kamath (Substack), Jul 2026"). It does not send emails or push notifications nudging people to trade (#source-14 "12 years of Zerodha - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Aug 2022"). Instead, from 2020 it added “nudges”, warnings that appear when a client is about to do something risky, such as buying an illiquid penny stock. Penny-stock trading on the platform fell by about 70%, Rest of World reported (#source-96 "Indian brokerage tries to disengage users (South Asia newsletter) - Rest of World, May 2022"). In June 2021 it added a “kill switch” that lets traders lock themselves out of a segment. “Over-trading is the biggest destroyer of capital when actively trading the markets,” Kamath wrote (#source-18 "Introducing Kill Switch - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Jun 2021").
“We, as a business, are taking the opposite stance, saying that people trading less is better for the trader,” he told Rest of World. “If you started with 100,000 rupees, and you lost 100,000 rupees, you will never come back to trade.” (#source-96 "Indian brokerage tries to disengage users (South Asia newsletter) - Rest of World, May 2022")
The firm stayed small. It has had about 1,000-1,200 employees for years (#source-15 "14 years of Zerodha - The Pivot? - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Sep 2024") (#source-95 "Nithin Kamath on how Zerodha built an $8 bn business with just 1,000 employees - Outlook Business, Jul 2026"), most of them working remotely after 2020 (#source-93 "Permanent remote work for 90% of Zerodha's workforce - HR Katha, May 2022"). “A nice place to work is not a perk we offer. It is kind of a business model in itself,” Kamath said in 2026 (#source-95 "Nithin Kamath on how Zerodha built an $8 bn business with just 1,000 employees - Outlook Business, Jul 2026"). He has paid staff a month’s salary for meeting a year-long fitness goal, with a Rs 10 lakh lucky draw on top. “Sitting is the new smoking,” he said (#source-92 "Burn 350 calories and get 1 month's salary: Nithin Kamath offers Rs 10 lakh reward - Business Today, Sep 2022").
It was also frugal. In 2022 he said Zerodha had enough money to run for more than 13 years with zero revenue and had always been debt-free. “We have been extremely frugal in how we operate.” (#source-14 "12 years of Zerodha - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Aug 2022")
Mutual funds and the money machine, 2023-2024
In August 2023 SEBI granted Zerodha a mutual fund licence, about three and a half years after it applied, for a joint venture with smallcase called Zerodha Fund House, led by Vishal Jain (#source-68 "Zerodha AMC gets mutual fund licence; Vishal Jain to head MF business - Business Standard, Aug 2023"). Its passive index funds and ETFs reached a quarterly average of about Rs 14,448 crore of assets by March 2026; the fund house was still loss-making in 2025-26 (#source-69 "Zerodha Fund House nearly triples assets as FY26 loss narrows - CXO Digitalpulse, Aug 2026").
The broking business, meanwhile, hit its peak. For 2023-24 Kamath’s own blog reported revenue of more than Rs 8,370 crore and profit of about Rs 4,700 crore, a profit margin of over 50% (#source-57 "Zerodha hits Rs 8,370 Cr revenue with over 50% profit margin in FY24 - Entrackr, Sep 2024"). Consolidated regulatory filings, which include other income and gains, showed revenue from operations of Rs 9,372 crore and profit of Rs 5,496 crore (#source-58 "Zerodha's revenue nears INR 10,000 Cr mark - Inc42, Dec 2024"). Either way, few Indian companies of any kind earn that much with so few people.
The family took a large share as pay. In 2021 the board approved a ceiling of up to Rs 100 crore a year each for Nithin, Nikhil and Seema Patil (#source-72 "Exclusive: Kamath brothers and Seema Patil to get up to Rs 100 Cr as salary - Entrackr, May 2021"). Actual pay in 2022-23 was Rs 72 crore each for the brothers and Rs 36 crore for Patil (#source-74 "Rs 72 crore was salary of Zerodha founders in FY 2022-23 - HR Katha, Dec 2023"); in 2024-25 it was Rs 96 crore each for the brothers (#source-60 "Zerodha cash reserve stands at Rs 22,679 Cr in FY25 - Entrackr, Nov 2025").
Losing the top spot
Growth had a limit. Kamath said in 2023 that active clients had been flat at about 64 lakh for about 18 months (#source-55 "Zerodha annual results: Nithin Kamath says 40% yearly jump in revenues in FY23 - Business Today, Sep 2023"). In September 2023, NSE data showed Groww, a venture-funded rival with an app built for first-time investors, had passed Zerodha: 66.3 lakh active clients against Zerodha’s 64.8 lakh (#source-50 "Groww topples Zerodha to become largest broker in terms of number of clients - Business Standard, Oct 2023").
The gap has widened since. In September 2026 Groww had 1.34 crore active NSE clients, about 29% of the market. Zerodha had 67.91 lakh (14.73%), only just ahead of Angel One’s 67.55 lakh (#source-51 "Groww adds over 1 lakh active clients in September 2026 - CXO Digitalpulse, Oct 2026"). Zerodha says it still accounts for over 15% of Indian retail trading volumes (#source-1 "About Zerodha - Zerodha, Oct 2026").
Rainmatter: the other portfolio
Kamath has said Zerodha sets aside a share of its earnings for startup investments and another share for social and environmental causes (#source-16 "15 years of Zerodha - The risk crystallises - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Sep 2025"). Rainmatter, the investing arm, had invested about Rs 400 crore in more than 80 startups by August 2023, when Zerodha committed another Rs 1,000 crore to it as a “perennial” fund with no fixed exit date (#source-23 "Rainmatter - Perennial investments - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Aug 2023"). By April 2026 it had put more than Rs 1,500 crore into over 160 startups, including 44 in climate and 41 in health and fitness. “We don’t take board seats,” Kamath said (#source-70 "Zerodha's Rainmatter invests INR 1,500 Cr across 160+ startups - Entrepreneur India, Apr 2026").
Recognition
In March 2025 Kamath was named EY Entrepreneur of the Year 2024 for India and went on to represent India at the World Entrepreneur of the Year event in Monaco (#source-36 "Nithin Kamath is the EY Entrepreneur of the Year 2024 - EY India, Mar 2025"). He also sits on SEBI’s Secondary Market Advisory Committee and Market Data Advisory Committee (#source-1 "About Zerodha - Zerodha, Oct 2026").
How the wealth is held
Kamath’s fortune is almost entirely his family’s stake in Zerodha, which is unlisted, plus Rainmatter’s investments and accumulated cash. Because there is no market price, published figures are estimates. Hurun put the Kamath brothers jointly at Rs 24,000 crore in 2020 (#source-97 "IIFL Wealth Hurun India Rich List: Kamath brothers top self-made chart with Rs 24,000 cr - Business Today, Oct 2020"). The Hurun India Rich List 2025 listed “Nithin Kamath & family” at rank 64 with Rs 40,020 crore (#source-98 "Ambani tops Hurun India Rich List 2025: top 100 richest Indians - Trak.in, Oct 2025") (#source-99 "Bengaluru's billionaire list: Azim Premji, Nithin Kamath and others - StartupTalky, Oct 2025"). Forbes’ real-time estimate on 13 October 2026 was US$4.7 billion (#source-37 "Nithin Kamath (real-time net worth profile) - Forbes, Oct 2026").
The setbacks and failures
Before Zerodha
The early record is a list of failures: a blown-up trading account built partly on borrowed money, a failed multi-level marketing venture, four years of night shifts to clear the debt, and a VC community that would not fund him (#source-2 "I am Nithin, and I founded Zerodha - nithinkamath.me, Jan 2021") (#source-44 "Zerodha's Nithin Kamath acknowledges father's role in the Kamath brothers' success - Storyboard18, Dec 2023") (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014"). “There is a science to it. I knew I would make up the money,” he later said of the trading losses (#source-43 "The Turning Point: what led Nithin Kamath to launch Zerodha - YourStory, Apr 2020").
The F&O squeeze, 2024-2026
Zerodha’s success rested heavily on active F&O traders. Industry analysis by Inc42 estimated that F&O accounted for nearly 90% of Zerodha’s revenue (#source-67 "Zerodha, Angel One, Groww feel the squeeze from SEBI crackdown - Inc42, Oct 2025"). In 2024 regulators moved to curb retail options trading.
From 1 October 2024, SEBI’s “true to label” rule ended the volume rebates that exchanges paid brokers like Zerodha, which Kamath said had been about 10% of revenue (#source-64 "'Will have to let go of zero brokerage': Nithin Kamath on SEBI's true-to-label move - Business Today, Jul 2024"). Then SEBI’s index-derivatives package cut weekly expiries to one index per exchange, raised contract sizes and tightened margins from November 2024 (#source-21 "SEBI's new rules for index derivatives: here's what's changing - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Oct 2024"). Kamath warned of a 30-50% hit (#source-59 "Zerodha profit jumps 61.5% in FY24; CEO warns of regulatory challenges - Business Standard, Sep 2024"). He kept delivery free (#source-100 "Nithin Kamath confirms free equity delivery - Outlook Money, Oct 2024"), but by June 2025 Zerodha’s brokerage revenue was down about 40% from a year earlier. “The risk has crystallised,” he wrote (#source-61 "Zerodha brokerage revenue drops 40% in Q1 FY26 - Entrackr, Sep 2025") (#source-16 "15 years of Zerodha - The risk crystallises - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Sep 2025").
For 2024-25, filings showed revenue down 11.5% to Rs 8,847 crore and profit down 22.9% to Rs 4,237 crore (#source-60 "Zerodha cash reserve stands at Rs 22,679 Cr in FY25 - Entrackr, Nov 2025"). In 2025-26 profit was flat at about Rs 4,283 crore, but brokerage income fell 10.7% to Rs 2,738 crore and interest income, mainly from margin lending, rose to Rs 2,269 crore (#source-62 "Zerodha's bland FY26: net profit up a mere 1% - Inc42, Aug 2026") (#source-63 "Zerodha marks 16 years with steady profits - YourStory, Aug 2026"). Kamath said revenue “hasn’t really grown in real terms” and that he was uneasy with how fast margin trading was growing (#source-62 "Zerodha's bland FY26: net profit up a mere 1% - Inc42, Aug 2026"). “With broking, we have to keep running just to stand still,” he wrote (#source-17 "16 years of Zerodha: Fresh enthusiasm - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Aug 2026").
In March 2026 Zerodha doubled its fee to Rs 40 per order for some intraday F&O trades where clients’ cash collateral is low, saying it had been funding the gap at a loss (#source-65 "Zerodha raises F&O charges to Rs 40 per order for certain intraday trades - Inc42, Mar 2026"). A month later Kamath said 60-70% of F&O volumes come from just 1-2% of traders (#source-66 "Nithin Kamath says 60-70% of F&O volumes come from just 1-2% traders - Business Today, Apr 2026").
Zero1 and other retreats
In April 2026 Zerodha shut Zero1, its personal-finance media and creator platform launched in 2023, citing “a lot of regulatory uncertainty” (#source-85 "Zerodha shuts down Zero1 - Entrepreneur India, Apr 2026") (#source-86 "Zero1 shutdown: what Zerodha's move signals for fintech platforms - Business Today, Apr 2026"). And Zerodha lost the No. 1 position by clients to Groww in 2023 and has not regained it (#source-50 "Groww topples Zerodha to become largest broker in terms of number of clients - Business Standard, Oct 2023") (#source-51 "Groww adds over 1 lakh active clients in September 2026 - CXO Digitalpulse, Oct 2026").
Controversies and allegations
Kamath and Zerodha have faced no criminal case, SEBI adjudication order or court finding of fraud that we could find in public records. The matters below are exchange and ministry penalties, a pay row, platform outages and public disputes. Each is set out with the response and the latest known status.
The Rs 100 crore pay ceiling (2021)
Allegation: In May 2021 Entrackr reported, from regulatory filings, that Zerodha’s board had approved annual pay of up to Rs 100 crore each for Nithin Kamath, Nikhil Kamath and Seema Patil (#source-72 "Exclusive: Kamath brothers and Seema Patil to get up to Rs 100 Cr as salary - Entrackr, May 2021"). The figure drew criticism on social media (#source-73 "Zerodha's Nithin Kamath clarifies on Rs100 crore salary after social media criticism - Moneylife, May 2021").
Response: Kamath clarified that the resolution set a ceiling and that actual pay was lower (#source-73 "Zerodha's Nithin Kamath clarifies on Rs100 crore salary after social media criticism - Moneylife, May 2021"). He pointed out that Zerodha’s profit for the year was about Rs 1,000 crore and that the firm was also running a Rs 200 crore employee stock buyback (#source-56 "Stock broking giant Zerodha's FY21 profit more than doubles to Rs 1,000 cr - Business Standard, May 2021").
What happened next:
 Filings later showed pay of Rs 72 crore each for the brothers in 2022-23 (#source-74 "Rs 72 crore was salary of Zerodha founders in FY 2022-23 - HR Katha, Dec 2023") and Rs 96 crore each in 2024-25 (#source-60 "Zerodha cash reserve stands at Rs 22,679 Cr in FY25 - Entrackr, Nov 2025").
Status: No regulatory issue arose. Pay remains within the approved limit and is disclosed in annual filings.
Trading platform outages (2019-2026)
Allegation: Traders have repeatedly complained of losses when Zerodha’s Kite platform failed during market hours, including a 35-40 minute outage on an F&O expiry day in August 2019 (#source-78 "F&O traders blindsided by technical glitch on Zerodha's digital platform - Business Standard, Aug 2019"), glitches on 6 November and 4 December 2023 (#source-19 "An apology for the two consecutive tech issues in the last two months - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Dec 2023"), and a January 2024 outage that made #BoycottZerodha trend on X (#source-79 "Boycott Zerodha trends: users express their disappointment over technical glitch - Storyboard18, Feb 2024"). A Kite outage on 3 February 2026, during a rally after the India-US trade deal, brought fresh demands for compensation (#source-81 "Zerodha down? Kite glitch hits traders as market rallies after India-US trade deal - Outlook Business, Feb 2026").
Response: Kamath publicly apologised for the late-2023 incidents, blaming a vendor’s anti-malware update and a faulty geo-IP database update, and asked affected clients to raise tickets for losses (#source-19 "An apology for the two consecutive tech issues in the last two months - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Dec 2023"). In 2024 he argued that the perception of frequent outages was amplified on social media, and CTO Kailash Nadh said exchange data showed Zerodha had among the fewest issues (#source-80 "Zerodha's 'frequent' tech glitches may be a perception problem, says management - Benzinga, Sep 2024"). Zerodha publishes a list of its own incidents (#source-20 "Transparency disclosures - Zerodha, Oct 2026").
What happened next:
 In October 2023 a BSE grievance committee found that Zerodha had ignored exchange alerts that its bandwidth use had crossed 70% during a July 2023 glitch, and ordered it to pay one trader Rs 8,225. Zerodha paid but its COO called part of the finding “a blatant mistake” (#source-77 "BSE committee blames Zerodha's inaction for tech glitch - Inc42, Oct 2023").
Status: Complaints are handled case by case; Zerodha has no blanket compensation policy. No regulator has penalised it over outages that we could find.
NSE penalties over “reversal trades” (2025-2026)
Allegation: In a series of disciplinary orders, NSE’s Member Committee examined “reversal trades”: trades in thinly traded options between related client accounts, where prices swing to move money from one account to another. The exchange found Zerodha’s monitoring inadequate in some cases, for example where linked clients traded from matching IP addresses (#source-6 "Member Committee order in the matter of Zerodha Broking Ltd (reversal trades, 2022) - NSE, Jun 2025"). It imposed penalties of Rs 92.06 lakh (order filed October 2025) (#source-7 "Member Committee order in the matter of Zerodha Broking Ltd (reversal trades, 2024) - NSE, Oct 2025"), Rs 19.02 lakh (May 2026) (#source-8 "Member Committee order in the matter of Zerodha Broking Ltd (reversal trades, 2023) - NSE, May 2026") and Rs 27.21 lakh (August 2026) (#source-9 "Member Committee order in the matter of Zerodha Broking Ltd (reversal trades, 2024) - NSE, Aug 2026"). The penalties were for weaknesses in Zerodha’s surveillance of its clients, not findings that Zerodha itself manipulated prices.
Response: Zerodha argued before the committee that it cannot always detect such trades when the counterparty is another broker’s client, that prices were within permitted ranges, and that it had blocked payouts and accounts once alerted. The committee accepted this in some cases and rejected it in others (#source-7 "Member Committee order in the matter of Zerodha Broking Ltd (reversal trades, 2024) - NSE, Oct 2025") (#source-8 "Member Committee order in the matter of Zerodha Broking Ltd (reversal trades, 2023) - NSE, May 2026") (#source-9 "Member Committee order in the matter of Zerodha Broking Ltd (reversal trades, 2024) - NSE, Aug 2026").
What happened next:
 Separately, a 2024 NSE order on a third-party YouTube video that promoted Zerodha found Zerodha had acted properly and imposed no penalty (#source-5 "Member Committee order in the matter of Zerodha Broking Ltd (advertisement code) - NSE, Apr 2024").
 NSE’s member directory lists no SEBI orders against Zerodha Broking (#source-4 "Member directory: Zerodha Broking Limited - National Stock Exchange of India, Oct 2026").
Status: Penalties were imposed by the exchange; we found no record of an appeal to the Securities Appellate Tribunal as of 13 October 2026.
Ministry penalty over a missing CFO (2024)
Allegation: The Registrar of Companies, under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, found that Zerodha Asset Management had gone 459 days (December 2021 to March 2023) without a chief financial officer, as the Companies Act requires. It fined the company and its officers Rs 23.98 lakh in total, including Rs 4.08 lakh on Kamath as a director (#source-75 "Zerodha along with its founder penalized by ROC for delay in appointing CFO - StudyCafe, Aug 2024") (#source-76 "Centre slaps Rs 4.08 lakh penalty on Zerodha co-founder Nithin Kamath for failing to appoint CFO - DNA, Aug 2024").
Response: The company had itself applied to settle the lapse. Its CEO said the gap related to the period before the fund house began operations (#source-75 "Zerodha along with its founder penalized by ROC for delay in appointing CFO - StudyCafe, Aug 2024").
Status: Penalties were levied in 2024; the matter is closed.
The “Zerodha scam” withdrawal row (2025)
Allegation: In November 2025 investor Aniruddha Malpani said on X that he could withdraw only Rs 5 crore a day from about Rs 42.9 crore in his account and called it a “scam” (#source-82 "'Zerodha scam': investor flags Rs 5-crore withdrawal rule; Nithin Kamath responds - Business Standard, Nov 2025").
Response: Kamath said his payouts had already been processed and that Rs 5 crore is an internal verification threshold because payouts cannot be reversed; larger withdrawals need a ticket (#source-82 "'Zerodha scam': investor flags Rs 5-crore withdrawal rule; Nithin Kamath responds - Business Standard, Nov 2025").
Status: Resolved; no regulatory action followed.
Impersonation and deepfakes (2023-present)
Allegation: This is a case where Kamath and Zerodha are targets, not accused. Fraudsters have run WhatsApp groups impersonating Kamath and COO Venu Madhav, using fake SEBI letters and a fake Kite app (#source-22 "Beware of investment scams in the name of Zerodha - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Nov 2024").
Response: Zerodha has issued public warnings, and in May 2025 Kamath said WhatsApp investment scams had “claimed the most victims” (#source-84 "Zerodha CEO Nithin Kamath alerts investors about WhatsApp investment scam - Outlook Money, May 2025"). In December 2023 he posted a deepfake video of himself to warn that AI could defeat online identity checks (#source-83 "Zerodha CEO Nithin Kamath shares his own deepfake video, warns about AI threats - Gulf News, Dec 2023").
Status: Ongoing; warnings continue. As of 13 October 2026 none of the matters above involves a pending criminal case against Kamath.
Giving back
A 25% pledge and a climate foundation
In 2021 the Kamath brothers pledged to give away 25% of their wealth during their lifetimes (#source-88 "Zerodha founders pledge to donate 25% of their wealth - The CSR Journal, Nov 2021"). Nithin’s main vehicle is the Rainmatter Foundation, which began with a commitment of about US$100 million in January 2021 for climate and ecology work. “What’s the point of fintech, without a planet to live on?” he asked at the time (#source-91 "Why Rainmatter decided to set up a $100 million foundation - YourStory, Jan 2021"). By September 2024 commitments to it were over Rs 1,000 crore (#source-15 "14 years of Zerodha - The Pivot? - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Sep 2024"); the foundation now describes a US$200 million commitment across ecology, livelihoods and community work (#source-26 "Rainmatter Foundation - rainmatter.org, Oct 2026"). “Wherever there is a concentration of wealth, the onus has to be to give back,” he wrote in 2022 (#source-14 "12 years of Zerodha - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Aug 2022").
To mark Zerodha’s 15th anniversary in September 2025, he announced the Rs 100 crore Zerodha Rewilding Fund. Its first project restores 800 acres near the Tadoba-Andhari tiger reserve in Maharashtra, with the state forest department and Farmers for Forests (#source-25 "Zerodha Rewilding Fund - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Sep 2025").
Covid relief and rankings
During the pandemic Zerodha set aside Rs 25 crore for Covid relief, including contributions to PM CARES, 15,000 meals a day in Bengaluru, a Covid hospital and a pilot of universal basic income (#source-27 "Zerodha Cares - COVID-19 relief - Zerodha, Oct 2026"). On the EdelGive Hurun India Philanthropy List, the brothers ranked ninth in 2022 with Rs 100 crore given (#source-89 "Kamath brothers among India's top 10 individual philanthropists; donations jump 308% - Business Today, Oct 2022") and gave Rs 110 crore in 2022-23 (#source-90 "Kamath brothers donated Rs 110 cr in FY23: EdelGive Hurun India Philanthropy List 2023 - Business Today, Nov 2023").
Nikhil, not Nithin, signed the Giving Pledge in 2023 (#source-38 "Nikhil Kamath (pledger letter) - The Giving Pledge, Jun 2023").
Free knowledge
Kamath’s longest-running gift may be Varsity, launched in 2014 on the principle that market knowledge “should have no ownership” (#source-11 "Introducing Varsity - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Nov 2014"). It remains free, for clients and non-clients alike.
Succession
Kamath has not named a successor. He told Outlook Business in 2025 that he spends his time making sure “there are 10-15 people in the business who understand the philosophy… and the decision-making framework” (#source-94 "Nithin Kamath interview: at the end of the day, you bet on founders - Outlook Business, Feb 2025"). The core team today is Nikhil Kamath (co-founder), Kailash Nadh (CTO), Venu Madhav (COO), Seema Patil (director) and Karthik Rangappa (chief of education) (#source-1 "About Zerodha - Zerodha, Oct 2026"). Ownership stays with the founders’ family, and with no outside investors or listing there is no external pressure on the question. “Usually people who come for money, go for money,” he said in the same interview. “The day you compromise on the philosophy, the culture suffers.” (#source-94 "Nithin Kamath interview: at the end of the day, you bet on founders - Outlook Business, Feb 2025")
What their journey teaches
Your first failure can be your best research. Kamath lost his savings trading, then spent years watching brokers from the inside as a sub-broker. Zerodha’s flat fee came from what he saw Reliance Money try and abandon (#source-39 "Why venture capitalists are flocking Zerodha today - The Economic Times, Sep 2014").
You can grow without outside money if you stay profitable from day one. Zerodha never raised venture capital (#source-33 "Inside the making of Zerodha - Nithin Kamath (Substack), Jul 2026"). “Not having to answer to investors… is a huge advantage,” Kamath said in 2026 (#source-71 "Rs 25,620 crore saved on brokerage: what Nithin Kamath wants you to know - Business Today, Apr 2026"). The cost was slower early years; the reward was control.
Giving something away can be the business model. Free equity delivery and free Varsity courses brought in long-term investors that advertising could not (#source-71 "Rs 25,620 crore saved on brokerage: what Nithin Kamath wants you to know - Business Today, Apr 2026") (#source-11 "Introducing Varsity - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Nov 2014").
Telling customers to do less can build trust. Nudges, a kill switch and blunt warnings about F&O losses ran against short-term revenue, and Kamath has said less than 1% of active traders earn more than a bank fixed deposit over three years (#source-101 "Less than 1% of stock traders make more returns than an FD over a 3-year period: Zerodha CEO - OfficeChai, Jan 2022") (#source-96 "Indian brokerage tries to disengage users (South Asia newsletter) - Rest of World, May 2022") (#source-18 "Introducing Kill Switch - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Jun 2021"). (For context on what a fixed deposit really earns, see CapitalVia’s look at FD real returns.)
Concentration is a risk even for the best. When regulators curbed F&O, a firm earning most of its money from a small group of active traders saw brokerage income fall. “Market cycles trump a lot of business decisions,” Kamath wrote (#source-16 "15 years of Zerodha - The risk crystallises - Z-Connect (Zerodha), Sep 2025").
A small team is a choice you have to keep making. Zerodha has stayed at about 1,000-1,200 people while serving crores of clients. “I never realised that more people also mean more inefficiencies,” Kamath said (#source-95 "Nithin Kamath on how Zerodha built an $8 bn business with just 1,000 employees - Outlook Business, Jul 2026").
Other self-built fortunes in Indian markets make useful comparisons: Uday Kotak built a broker into a bank, and Radhakishan Damani went from trading floor to retail.
A profile for general reading, based on public records and reporting as of 13 October 2026. Not investment, tax or legal advice.

Frequently asked questions
Who is Nithin Kamath?
Nithin Kamath is the founder and CEO of Zerodha, the Bengaluru-based discount stock broker he started on 15 August 2010. He built it without venture capital, advertising or a sales team, and it now has more than 1.8 crore clients.
What is Nithin Kamath's net worth in 2026?
Forbes estimated Nithin Kamath's net worth at about US$4.7 billion on 13 October 2026. The Hurun India Rich List 2025 placed 'Nithin Kamath & family' at rank 64 with Rs 40,020 crore. His wealth is mainly the family's stake in unlisted Zerodha, so all figures are estimates.
How did Nithin Kamath start Zerodha?
Kamath began trading at about 17, lost his savings in the early 2000s and worked night shifts at a call centre while trading by day. He then managed money for clients, became a Reliance Money sub-broker in 2006, and launched Zerodha in 2010 with his own savings, his brother Nikhil and a flat Rs 20 per order fee.
Where is Nithin Kamath from?
He was [personal detail removed]ly. His father worked at Canara Bank and the family later settled in Bengaluru, where Zerodha is based.
What is Nithin Kamath's education?
He studied engineering at Bangalore Institute of Technology. By his own account he never cleared the backlog of papers needed to complete the degree, and he has no management degree.
Has Zerodha or Nithin Kamath faced any controversy?
There is no criminal case or SEBI order against him on record. Controversies include the 2021 board approval of pay of up to Rs 100 crore a year for the founders, repeated trading-platform outages, NSE penalties on Zerodha for weak monitoring of clients' reversal trades, and a 2024 ministry fine over a missing CFO at Zerodha's fund house.
Who will succeed Nithin Kamath at Zerodha?
No successor has been named. Kamath has said he is building a group of 10-15 leaders who understand Zerodha's philosophy; the core team includes co-founder Nikhil Kamath, CTO Kailash Nadh, COO Venu Madhav, director Seema Patil and Karthik Rangappa.
Is Zerodha listed on the stock market?
No. Zerodha is privately owned by its founders and has never raised outside capital. Kamath has repeatedly said he has no plans for an IPO.

Nithin Kamath, Founder and CEO of Zerodha is now a nominated non-official member of the government's reconstituted National Start-up Advisory Council (NASC). The Centre on December 18 announced 31 such new members. Constituted under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), it will be led by Union Minister Piyush Goyal.
Announcing the same via social media site X (formerly Twitter), Kamath wrote: "More Indians today than ever before are aspiring to be entrepreneurs thanks to government initiatives and messaging, the media coverage of the start-up ecosystem, founder success stories, and more. The one thing we need to work on as a nation is to unlock domestic capital for start-ups/MSMEs. Reduce the dependence on foreign capital and get Indians to back Indian start-ups."
On what he aims to pursue, Kamath said, “It is maybe time for newer products or vehicles that can be used by accredited investors or those who can take higher risks to be able to invest in equity or debt in start-ups/MSMEs. The appetite in India to invest in newer products is like never before and we need to make use of this opportunity. Apart from reducing external capital dependency, this could also mean that wealth created from startups stays in India.”
National Start-up Advisory Council
The NASC was originally constituted in January 2020 to advise the government on measures needed to build a strong ecosystem for nurturing innovation and start-ups in the country.
The term of non-official members of the council was for two years. Since the term of two years is now complete, the central government nominates non-official members on the council representing various stakeholders such as founders of successful startups, veterans who have grown and scaled companies in India, persons capable of representing the interest of investors in startups, and representatives of associations, the DPIIT said in a statement.
The nominated non-official members include Prof Amitabha Bandyopadhyay, IIT Kanpur, Karthik Reddy, Indian Venture and Alternate Capital Association, Prof Yogesh Singh, University of Delhi, Nithin Kamath, from Zerodha, Nivruti Rai from Invest India, and presidents of industry chambers like CII.
The eighth meeting of the NSAC was held under the chairmanship of the commerce and industry minister on December 19.
The council meets regularly to suggest measures such as fostering a culture of innovation among citizens and students in particular; and promoting innovation in all sectors of the economy across the country, including semiurban and rural areas.

Blume Podcast | Season 4   Podcast
Nithin Kamath of Zerodha on bootstrapping his way to build the largest online brokerage in India
 
Nithin Kamath
 
Karthik Reddy
Episode
:   S2 E3
Published
Reading Time
:   34 minutes
In this episode, Nithin Kamath, founder and CEO of Zerodha sat down with Karthik B. Reddy, Managing Partner at Blume Ventures, to talk about building and scaling an online brokerage firm without any external capital.   
He emphasizes the importance of building trust before buying a financial product, which is built through word of mouth. They have worked on building trust by answering customer queries on forums and providing market intelligence.  
Highlighting Zerodha’s self-sustainability, Nithin argues that having growth capital could have allowed them to grow faster, but also acknowledges it still happened at the same pace nevertheless minus the pressure of raising one round after the other.
Takeaways
Nithin discusses the importance of long-term thinking in business, contrasting with other peers who focus on short-term goals. At Zerodha, the core team has been together for at least five or six years, ensuring their understanding of the business and skill sets compound over time. This approach has kept the business together, as the top hundred members are dedicated to the company’s philosophies, such as treating customers right and using success to give forward.
> Our philosophy is to always think of the customer first. We focus on building products and services that we would want to use ourselves.
Nithin Kamath, Founder & CEO - Zerodha
Karthik: My guest today needs no introduction. Nithin Kamath has been recognized as one of the most influential entrepreneurs of the last decade. He’s been associated with startups, but he’s an established business today. Winner of numerous business awards, primarily because he’s built a robust, profitable business without any external capital.
And his journey, along with his brother, has been a great journey of entrepreneurship. A product which came and disrupted the industry that he was working in. And on this episode of the Blume Podcast, we would love to hear more about Nithin’s story, his motivations, his ability to sort of persevere through this decade plus journey, and how he built this massive business without outside capital.
And most importantly, for all the young listeners out there and entrepreneurs who are aspiring to be someone like Nithin Kamath — What lessons can he impart? And, of course, he is a great example of the theme of this year’s podcast, which is the power of compounding, and you’ve seen that impact as he rose up the ranks and became the leading brokerage in the country.
Karthik: So welcome again, Nithin, lovely to have you on the podcast and thanks for taking the time.
Nithin: My pleasure. Thanks for having me.
Karthik: Yeah, so let’s get going. I think the first segment I want to cover a little bit of the backstory. I know it’s well documented. There are many versions of it that are already there in the public domain.
But while the story is documented and you’ve bootstrapped this into a… anybody’s guess on how valuable it is on any given day… it’s clearly a multibillion dollar company. It’s taken over a decade. But what would be most interesting is, I think, when you look at the venture lens today, we keep questioning these young founders, how do you build…how does this become a billion dollar business?

No, I think a lot of people have always wondered whether they can be a small shareholder and aspiration wise you’ve given them hope to look forward to that in a few years from now. So that’s great. So I think we already, in the last two questions, quietly segued into what you’ve achieved in terms of the power of compounding, which is the theme for the podcast series this year. And what it may look like when you start compounding Zerodha for the next few decades at least, right? That’s already a great segue, and I have a bunch of questions before we wrap this up. The first of those is, as much as you are a trader and as much as you’ve built the firm on that strong product linkage with your love for trading, do you also invest in public stocks? And if there are, out of curiosity, given that your wealth compounds in your own organization, are there examples of public stocks that you can share where wealth is compounded faster than your own efforts or where there have been great examples of this? And how have you judged that from the outside?
Nithin: No, all the public market investment, actually, Nikhil handles, and he’s been quite special in terms of his performance over the last 13 years and…
Karthik: I’ve heard, yes, I’ve heard good, great things about it.
Nithin: Like I said, one of the reasons we didn’t have to go out and raise venture capital right at the start was because he was sitting and trading the markets and generating returns for us to be able to take the stance because I think the business on its own started generating cash only in 2013. So the first two, three years really, we survived out of these trading profits. So in a way, if you were to think of it, that capital that he brought in because of trading, it is almost invaluable for us, and that has probably outperformed everything else. But yeah, but during the last few years, we’ve been holding a bunch of stocks. We have a lot of exposure to banks over the last two, three years. We also sit on a lot of gold because we are already overexposed to the equity markets. So we have quite a bit of sovereign gold bonds in our portfolio.
Karthik: Understood. That’s your investment mix. But if I bring it back to how you’ve compounded value for your current set of shareholders, which is also your team, etc., any one example where you’ve…You’ve judged and seen that be successful in the public markets. You’re saying, let’s leave that answer to Nikhil, but let me then switch gears and come to the startups that you back. And I know you do a lot of that, right? And what indicators are you looking for from these founders? I know it’s very similar to how we are judging, but how do you know these people are likely to be winners in that power of compounding game?
Of course, we’re going to get some wrong for various reasons, right? But how do you differentiate compounding and non-compounding if there is a startup founder who pitches to you? If you don’t have a view on the public one necessarily.
Nithin: So we’ve stuck around our core competency. It’s around finance, investing, trading, and the stock market. All the private investments in this space mostly, I think we have invested, I think 400 – 500 crores till now. And it’s across 80 – 90 startups.
Karthik: Oh, wow. I didn’t realize that it becomes that big.
It’s more than our portfolio now. It’s great that you’re doing this. This is what we love to see, right? More people enabling more startups. But yeah…
Nithin: For example, Smallcase really, was our first investment, right? And so when the founders came, they understood the market. They had a product that was solving a real market problem. They seemed like decent guys, and we knew that we could bring some strategic value to them. So in finance, it’s actually been quite easy because we know that almost every investment we make, more than the value we bring in terms of monetary capital, we bring a lot more value in terms of having the experience of having done this. Navigating regulations, providing quick opportunities for someone building a consumer-facing app, because the way we have done this for a lot of… Like even for Smallcase, for example, when they first conceptualized the product, we showcased it to our customers as if it’s our own product.
So in a way, we helped them achieve what would otherwise have taken maybe two, three years to get to, probably accelerating it for them. So we bring a lot of value. So what happens in FinTech, especially around saving and trading, is that anytime someone out there is starting something, we automatically get the deal flow.
Karthik: Correct. You’ve done this before, and you’ve established a track record of actually enabling this for many startups… and they are all accessible. You’ve backed some great founders who, in some sense .. I know you’re not saying it overtly.. You’ve backed founders who also think open source. They’re giving back, they’re helping other founders, and that’s how I’ve seen it flow from the Smallcase founders, etc. If it’s happening for me, I’m sure it’s happening tenfold for you, given how focused you are on what you chase.
Nithin: And then it extended into health. I’m passionate about health, fitness, nutrition. I think Indians should play more sports. So the instincts don’t play as well here as in finance. Yeah. But that’s why I think we’re still writing smaller cheques, etc. We’re trying to figure it out before we start committing larger capital. The final theme is really around climate change and the creation of livelihood. So we set up a foundation…
Karthik: I’d love to hear what motivated that, and I know it’s a personal passion, and all of them seem to be driven by personal passion, but please maybe spend a few minutes on what you’re trying to actually impact on climate change with this huge corpus that you’ve set aside.
Nithin:  Well, it all started with Kailash questioning internally, saying that success, the financial success, also brings some kind of an obligation to help society in some way, right? These kinds of questions started, and then we realized that in a world as unequal as it is today, people who have become wealthy should do more to give back. Otherwise, wealth will just keep concentrating, right? So we started with that idea. Through Rainmatter, we were already giving back by supporting entrepreneurs. We were closely associated with two problem statements: one around climate change and two around creating livelihoods. Even within our business, we realized that as we become more efficient, we indirectly cause job losses in the industry. Today, we have 1,100 people, but if Zerodha was not as efficient as it is, we might have needed 11,000 people. So we decided to pick up these two themes and support anyone working to solve these problems, whether for profit or nonprofit. We set up the foundation and allocated a thousand crores to start. We’re helping nonprofits and for-profits in this space. Any upside from the for-profits goes back to the foundation. This approach also helps keep the team together, knowing that the business is using its success to give back.
Karthik: I think there was an important lesson there. Many founders and wealth creators talk about wanting to give back, and I heard that in the first part of your answer. But reading between the lines, my takeaway is that you want even that giving to compound in some sense. Chasing things that truly align with what you want to see in the world. All the things you mentioned about your team falling in love with it, having a passion to solve these problems, will allow that giving-back to compound. So we keep going back to the principles of change agents and what impact we can create, whether it’s as a VC, as Nithin and Zerodha, or through the foundation. The motivation to compound is fantastic, and you’re doing it across the core business, investing side — we’ve seen in 7 years you have gone from 0 to 80 odd investments, and the foundation with a focus on environmental impact.
You’ve effectively used media for personal branding and, more importantly, for the right kind of messaging… What message do you want to send out into the world.. How important do you think this is for startup founders in general? I understand that not everyone can do it, but people can learn, as we all aren’t founders or CEOs by definition. We train ourselves for these roles because they come with responsibilities. So, do you have any tips on how to get started or how to compound your media presence? It’s evident that you’ve done it very well when we look at your team, product, customers, revenues, profits, and your initiatives outside of the core business. It seems to be central to your DNA, Nithin. That’s my read. So, I’m summarizing this for the audience and then moving on to some lighter questions about how founders should think about compounding their media presence.
Nithin: I think so. I blew up my trading account in 2001, and I joined a call-center, where I worked for three to four years between 2001 and 2004 – 2005. Even before the call center job and during my time there, I was also involved in multi-level marketing, trying to essentially sell.
Reflecting on my journey, I believe I learned most of my life skills during that time. As a founder and CEO, storytelling is crucial, especially for consumer startups. Building a brand for a business is challenging without the founder’s involvement in storytelling. As we spoke about earlier, back in 2013 – 2014, I realized that if we were to raise venture capital, it might limit the kinds of stories I could tell.
In my view, as a business, you should be able to say and do things that are difficult for your competition to say-and-do. Social media is incredibly powerful today. I was actually late to the game, only joining Twitter and LinkedIn in 2019. Until then, I managed everything through Zerodha itself, operating under the company’s handles and engaging with forums.
I used to spend a lot of time meeting with journalists. I don’t know how many India-darshans I’ve done. Just meeting journalists across the country to build Zerodha’s story in the press. However, I realized that the power of traditional press was waning around 2017 – 2018, and the reach of business handles on social media was decreasing as well, requiring advertising for visibility. So in 2019, I started using Twitter more actively. One challenge with social media is that it can give you dopamine hits, so it’s important to be conscious of that. In our office, there are three people who have the authority to approve or disapprove anything I want to say. I send my thoughts to them before posting, and unless they approve, it doesn’t go through. It’s a great system because it prevents me from impulsively saying things I shouldn’t.
I usually write down my thoughts, think about them, and sleep on them. If I still feel it’s worth saying the next day, then I go ahead. It’s not about firing off random tweets or posts; there’s a lot of thought and consideration behind what I share. This approach allows me to address topics that others may find challenging to discuss given their positions as entrepreneurs. It also helps me build an audience.
Karthik: That’s a tough one, especially for people who’ve already taken the money! But I think the other tips are very valuable. Interestingly, there’s another parallel in our lives. I managed all the way until 2014 – 2015 for Blume Ventures. I didn’t have a personal handle until around 2015. In fact, I didn’t even have a handle, let alone tweeting. My account was created much later, well after Blume Ventures. So I believe in everything you’ve said. Thanks for sharing your insights.
You’re building toward that IPO, and you understand what public markets and investors want. As parting advice for founders, I think there’s going to be a flood of companies wanting to go public. This idea has gained traction over the last week. There are other success stories in the small-cap and mid-cap space. Personally, I want to harp on these success stories and showcase them as role models.
With all the knowledge you have, if you were an investor in their IPOs, what advice would you give these founders?
Nithin: I think the problem is that many founders are primed to view an IPO as an exit. However, it’s actually the beginning of a new journey for the founder. It involves getting retail investors who can’t take as much risk. Retail investors are at the bottom of the risk hierarchy when it comes to capital. So your obligation only increases, not decreases. This mental framework needs to change. People should see the money retail investors put into their company as an obligation rather than viewing it as an exit strategy — where you are trying to optimise for the exit
Another thing I’ve noticed is that, as a private company, there’s sometimes an incentive to oversell. But as a public company, it’s always better to promise less and overdeliver. Overselling can come back to haunt you, and you need to maintain the right mindset to run a business in the long run. You don’t want volatility. To reduce volatility and increase the likelihood of making rational decisions in the future, it’s better to constantly underpromise and overdeliver.
I think these two things are crucial.
Karthik: This example that you gave of underselling and outperforming, I’ve seen it in action the most… I don’t follow public markets much, but I’ve always been intrigued by DMART because we look at a lot of players in that segment. We had invested in Milk Basket & Dunzo. So I got intrigued, and of course, Damani Ji is not very visible, but Neville is at the front, and he does a fantastic job of this. He takes two, three hours every quarter to talk to analysts, walk them through the journey. He keeps it very humble and very real, and then just keeps outperforming, right? It’s an amazing story. And I’m sure Zerodha will be a public story of the same nature someday. We know the man behind it thinks this way. So a big thanks for giving us that philosophy that guides you and what to expect the day we can all be public shareholders in Zerodha. Thanks again, Nithin. Thank you for your time today. It was an incredible conversation. I enjoy these because I get to interact with some of the best founders in the country. I love tracking these decade-plus, two-decade-plus journeys. I’m sure you’ve inspired a lot of our listeners, motivated them to think long-term, build sustainable businesses, and see what compounding can do. And that’s the message we want to send out this season. So thank you once again.

Founder & CEO, Zerodha; Pioneer of Discount Broking in India; Expert in FinTech and Wealth Democratization
Nithin Kamath is a seminal entrepreneur and technologist who is the Founder and CEO of Zerodha, a company that has fundamentally transformed the Indian stock broking industry. Bootstrapped in 2010 to overcome the hurdles he faced as a trader, his career is a masterclass in leveraging innovation and a deep understanding of customer pain points to drive market disruption.
Kamath's success is rooted in his strategic approach to market access, which he captured in the company name: Zerodha (a blend of "Zero" and "Rodha," meaning barrier). He revolutionized stock trading by introducing a flat-fee model of just INR 20 per trade, enabling millions of ordinary Indians to participate in wealth creation through equity markets. This disruptive pricing and technology-first approach propelled Zerodha to handle approximately 15% of India’s daily trading volume with over 1.6 crore users.
His mission extends beyond profit to include financial literacy. Through initiatives like Varsity, Zerodha has provided educational resources that have improved the knowledge base of retail investors, creating a more informed participant base in India’s capital markets. This dedication to industry development is formally recognized by his membership on the SEBI Secondary Market Advisory Committee (SMAC) and the Market Data Advisory Committee (MDAC).
As a speaker and thought leader, Kamath's philosophy includes the practical "1% rule" for wealth creation, which focuses on consistent, automated investing. His presentations offer invaluable lessons for new and aspiring entrepreneurs on identifying customer pain points, harnessing technology for disruption, and achieving successful growth in competitive fintech environments.

Nithin Kamath (born 5 October 1979) is an Indian entrepreneur and the founder and chief executive officer (CEO) of Zerodha.
Early life and education
[edit]
Kamath was [personal detail removed]. His father, U. R. Kamath, worked as an executive at Canara Bank, and his mother, Revathi, was a veena teacher. He has a younger brother, Nikhil Kamath, who later became his business partner. The family relocated to Bangalore in 1996.
Career
[edit]
Kamath began trading in the stock market at the age of 17, initially managing his father's trading account. From January 1997 to January 2004, he worked as a self-employed proprietary trader. To supplement his income, he worked as a Senior Tele-sales Associate at a call centre from January 2001 to January 2004, trading during the day and working nights.
From January 2004 to January 2010, Kamath worked as a sub-broker for Kamath Associates, a franchise of Reliance Money, where he provided portfolio advisory services and engaged in proprietary trading.
Founding of Zerodha
[edit]
In 2010, Kamath co-founded Zerodha with his brother Nikhil Kamath. The company introduced a discount broking model in India, offering a flat fee of ₹20 per trade regardless of order size, in contrast to percentage-based fee structures used by traditional brokers.
The discount-broking model contributed to the firm's growth without significant spending on advertising or venture-capital funding. By 2020, Zerodha reported a self-assessed valuation of approximately US$1 billion.
Other ventures
[edit]
In 2015, Kamath founded Rainmatter, a fintech fund and incubator that supports startups working in financial technology. He also co-founded True Beacon, an investment management firm, together with Nikhil Kamath.
Personal life
[edit]
Nithin Kamath married Seema Patil in 2008. They have a son named Kiaan.
